abstract: We introduce the Poisson Super Learner, a scalable ensemble method for survival and competing risks prediction with right-censored data. The approach exploits the correspondence between the likelihood of piecewise-constant hazard models and the Poisson likelihood. After expanding the data over a chosen time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a common Poisson loss, and cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta learner. The resulting ensemble is a geometric combination of candidate hazards, and can be used to estimate survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks. The Poisson Super Learner framework is modular and can in principle incorporate any learner that can estimate interval-specific hazards, including parametric, penalised, additive, and other machine-learning hazard models. Training targets the cause-specific hazard directly and does not require explicit modelling of the censoring distribution. For competing risks, separate cause-specific ensembles are fitted and subsequently combined to obtain individualised cumulative incidence predictions. We illustrate the approach using data from the Steno Diabetes Center collected between 2005 and 2022 to predict cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes from detailed covariate information. The applied analysis is complemented by simulation studies designed to reflect key features of the data and to examine the behaviour of the method under controlled settings. All analyses were implemented using the freely available R software package poissonsuperlearner.

sections.body: Individual absolute risk at a horizon is built from cause-specific hazards, so the task is choosing among candidate hazard estimators for prediction. The paper proposes the Poisson Super Learner. Follow-up is split into intervals with piecewise-constant hazards, so the counting-process likelihood matches a Poisson likelihood. Candidate learners are trained under one cross-validated criterion, and a Poisson meta learner combines their log-hazard predictions. The text contrasts this with earlier super learners for censored data, which use discrete-time binary outcomes, Cox partial likelihoods, integrated Brier scores, pseudo-observations, or joint censoring models. The stated contributions are the Poisson formulation, the geometric meta learner, and the extension to cause-specific ensembles for competing risks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Poisson Super Learner ensembles candidate hazard learners on a discretized time scale for survival and competing-risks prediction.

sections.body: The construction has two stages. First, each base learner is trained by cross-validation under the Poisson likelihood loss, and its cross-validated log-hazard predictions are stored. Second, a Poisson meta learner is fitted on those predictions, giving a geometric ensemble of the candidate hazards. The steps are: choose a horizon $\tau$, partition the interval from zero to $\tau$, split the data into V folds, and re-estimate each base learner on the full data. For a new observation, each base learner's hazard is predicted, combined using the meta learner weights, and mapped to absolute risks at $\tau$. Without competing risks, survival probability is one minus the absolute risk.
sections.heading: Overview of the Poisson Super Learner
sections.headline: Candidate hazard learners are trained under Poisson loss, combined by a Poisson meta learner, and mapped to absolute risks.

sections.body: Covariates, event times, censoring times and event types are observed as right-censored data. Censoring is assumed conditionally independent of event time and type given covariates. Each cause-specific hazard is piecewise constant over the time partition, and each interval contributes a Poisson log-likelihood with event indicator $D_{i,k,j}$ and time at risk $R_{i,k}$. The loss is the negative of this log-likelihood, and each candidate learner minimises its empirical risk. The interval hazard is `lambda_{j,k}(x)` equal to the exponential of a learner-specific function of covariates. Parametric learners include log-linear generalised linear models with elastic-net constraints, and generalised additive models with penalised spline smooth terms. Any learner that returns interval-specific hazards on the partition can enter the library.
sections.heading: General framework
sections.headline: Piecewise-constant cause-specific hazards give a Poisson log-likelihood, with censoring assumed conditionally independent of event time.

sections.body: Each candidate learner is refitted on training folds and predicts log-hazards for the held-out fold, so every prediction comes from models estimated without that individual. Folds are defined at subject level, so all rows for one person stay in the same split. Tuning inside each learner uses only the training data of that split. The stacked predictions form level-one data for each cause, keeping the event indicators and times at risk and replacing covariates with the cross-validated log-hazards. Computation time increases with the number of intervals, folds, causes and learners. Sensitivity to the number of intervals and folds is reported in the supplementary material, not in this section.
sections.heading: V-Fold Cross-Validation
sections.headline: Cross-validated log-hazard predictions are made at subject level so each individual is held out from its own training folds.

sections.body: The meta learner is a Poisson regression on level-one data with one coefficient $\alpha_j^s$ per base learner. The coefficients are the same across time intervals, which keeps the model low-dimensional and avoids interval-specific weights. The ensemble hazard is the product over learners of each base hazard raised to its coefficient, so with nonnegative coefficients it is a weighted geometric product. The text contrasts this with the arithmetic mixture used by the standard Super Learner. Coefficients are estimated by minimising the empirical Poisson loss on the level-one data. The stated limitation is that time-varying coefficients would add parameters and could be unstable in intervals with few events.
sections.heading: The meta learner
sections.headline: A time-invariant Poisson meta learner combines base-learner log-hazards into a geometric ensemble hazard.

sections.body: The discrete Poisson Super Learner does not combine learners. For each cause, it selects the single learner with the lowest cross-validated Poisson loss across the V folds. The selection sums the loss over held-out observations in each fold and divides by n. The chosen learner is then refitted on all n observations and used for prediction. In the Steno application, the discrete version had lower prediction accuracy than the ensemble at every horizon. In the simulations, it was close to the strongest full-library learners at larger sample sizes.
sections.heading: The Discrete Poisson Super Learner
sections.headline: The discrete version selects one learner per cause by minimum cross-validated Poisson loss instead of ensembling.

sections.body: For a new covariate vector, each base learner, refitted on the full sample, gives a log-hazard in each interval. The ensemble hazard in each interval is the exponential of the meta learner coefficients times these log-hazards, summed over learners. Survival probability at time t is the exponential of minus the sum of cumulative cause-specific hazards over all causes. The absolute risk for cause j is an explicit sum over intervals. Each term weights the survival at the interval start by the cause's share of the total hazard, times one minus the exponential of minus total hazard times the time spent in the interval. Zero divided by zero is set to zero. The closed-form derivation is given in the supplementary material.
sections.heading: Predictions on new data
sections.headline: Predicted hazards for new covariates combine full-sample base learners, and risks follow from explicit interval formulas.

sections.body: Two simulated competing-risks scenarios share covariates, censoring and the competing hazard. In Scenario Alpha the cause 1 hazard is linear in the covariates. In Scenario Beta, hinge-squared terms for age and LDL cholesterol are added. The full library has unpenalised, lasso, ridge and additive learners, and the linear library drops the additive one. External benchmarks are a Cox model, a joint survival learner, a continuous-time survival Super Learner, and a pseudo-observation Super Learner. The Cox benchmark was specified using knowledge of the simulation design. Performance is the index of prediction accuracy (IPA), a scaled Brier score, at 5 years, on a test sample of 10000, averaged over 80 replicates.
sections.heading: Simulation study
sections.headline: In simulations, the ensemble matched the strongest component learner and library choice mattered under nonlinear hazards.

sections.body: The data are 4821 adult patients with type 1 diabetes from Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen, followed up until 30 April, 2022. Training uses 3583 observations from 2005 to 2014, and the test set uses 1238 observations from 2015 to 2022. The event is first cardiovascular disease, with non-cardiovascular death as the competing event. Cause 1 uses the linear library. Cause 2 uses a generalised linear model and an additive model with a spline in age, because few subjects have the competing event. Table 3 shows Ridge best at horizons 1, 4 and 5, GAM best at 6 and 7, and the cause-specific Cox model best at 2 and 3. The ensemble is close to the best individual model at several horizons but is never the top model. These are single-split results.
sections.heading: Data application on the real data
sections.headline: In the Steno type 1 diabetes application, the ensemble stayed close to the best individual model across horizons.

sections.body: The paper concludes that the ensemble performed similarly to the strongest candidate in its library across the investigated settings. A linear library sufficed for an approximately linear hazard, while an additive learner helped when effects were nonlinear. The method remained competitive with survival Super Learner approaches and proportional-hazards benchmarks, and kept a likelihood interpretation on the hazard scale. The relative computational cost of Poisson-based models fell as sample size grew. A stated limitation is that meta learner coefficients are time-invariant; time-varying coefficients would add parameters and may be unstable where events are few. Suggested extensions include Highly Adaptive Lasso and eXtreme Gradient Boosting learners.
sections.heading: Discussion and conclusions
sections.headline: The ensemble matched its strongest candidates in the tested settings, with time-varying meta learners proposed as a future extension.

sections.body: This appendix contains the closed-form derivation of predicted risks under piecewise-constant cause-specific hazards, extra simulation details, and supplementary results for the real-data application. It also covers sensitivity to the number of intervals and folds, and computation times. Analyses used version 0.2.0 of the R package `poissonsuperlearner`, available on CRAN. Simulations were implemented with the targets workflow manager. Replication code and instructions are at gpitt71/replication-material-psl, and further material is on the project website.
sections.heading: Supplementary material
sections.headline: The appendix contains closed-form risk derivations, simulation details, supplementary real-data results, and software details.
